current_example.title: Example: Calculating the Shortest Distance Between an Osculating Plane and the Origin

q-77651.name: Question 1
q-77651.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0$, given that

$$
r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,T(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩
$$

where $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-77651.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point that is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$ The unit tangent vector $T(0)$ and the principal normal vector $N(0)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as 

$$
R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0),\,s,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,{e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(1,\,0,\,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0) \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩+s\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩+u\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{3}},\,\frac{s}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}},\,1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve r(t) at the point where t=0, given that

r(t)=⟨et,etsin⁡t,etcos⁡t⟩,T(0)=13⟨1,1,1⟩,N(0)=12⟨0,1,−1⟩

where T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
R(s,u)=⟨s3,s3+u2,u2⟩
b
R(s,u)=⟨2+s3,1−u2,3+s3−u2⟩
c
R(s,u)=⟨1+s3−u2,1−s3,1−u2⟩
d
R(s,u)=⟨1+3s,2s+3u,2s−3u⟩
e
R(s,u)=⟨1+s3,s3+u2,1+s3−u2⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The osculating plane passes through the point that is at the tip of the vector r(0). The unit tangent vector T(0) and the principal normal vector N(0) are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0),s,u∈(−∞,∞).

We have that

r(0)=⟨e0,e0sin⁡0,e0cos⁡0⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩.

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point (1,0,1) is given by

R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0)=⟨1,0,1⟩+s⋅13⟨1,1,1⟩+u⋅12⟨0,1,−1⟩=⟨1+s3,s3+u2,1+s3−u2⟩

q-127137.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{3},\,2-{t}^{2},\,t⟩,\,T(0)=⟨0,0,1⟩,\,N(0)=⟨0,-1,0⟩.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-127137.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P$, which is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$ The vectors $T(0)$ and $N(0)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{3},\,2-{0}^{2},\,0⟩=⟨0,2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(0,2,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0) \\  & =⟨0,2,0⟩+s⟨0,0,1⟩+u⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2-u,\,s⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
R(s,u)=⟨1,s−u,2u⟩
b
R(s,u)=⟨u,2+s,3u⟩
c
R(s,u)=⟨0,2−u,s⟩
d
R(s,u)=⟨0,u+s,1⟩
e
R(s,u)=⟨0,1+u,s−1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The osculating plane passes through the point P, which is at the tip of the vector r(0). The vectors T(0) and N(0) are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0),s,u∈(−∞,∞).

We have that r(0)=⟨03,2−02,0⟩=⟨0,2,0⟩.

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point (0,2,0) is given by R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0)=⟨0,2,0⟩+s⟨0,0,1⟩+u⟨0,−1,0⟩=⟨0,2−u,s⟩.

q-127278.name: Question 3
q-127278.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,T(0)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨-1,-1,1⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨0,-1,-1⟩.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-127278.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P$, which is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$ The vectors $T(0)$ and $N(0)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩=⟨0,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(0,1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0) \\  & =⟨0,1,1⟩+s\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨-1,-1,1⟩+u\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨0,-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3},\,1-\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3}-\frac{u\sqrt{2}}{2},\,1+\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3}-\frac{u\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve r(t) at the point where t=0, given that r(t)=⟨t,cos⁡t−sin⁡t,cos⁡t+sin⁡t⟩,T(0)=33⟨−1,−1,1⟩,N(0)=22⟨0,−1,−1⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
 R(s,u)=⟨−s33,u22,s33−1⟩
b
R(s,u)=⟨3,(s−u)3,(s+u)3⟩
c
 R(s,u)=⟨1+s33,1−u22,s33−u22⟩
d
R(s,u)=⟨3,(s+u)3,(s−u)3⟩

EXPLANATION

The osculating plane passes through the point P, which is at the tip of the vector r(0). The vectors T(0) and N(0) are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0),s,u∈(−∞,∞).

We have that r(0)=⟨0,cos⁡0−sin⁡0,cos⁡0+sin⁡0⟩=⟨0,1,1⟩.

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point (0,1,1) is given by R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0)=⟨0,1,1⟩+s⋅33⟨−1,−1,1⟩+u⋅22⟨0,−1,−1⟩=⟨−s33,1−s33−u22,1+s33−u22⟩.

q-78207.name: Question 4
q-78207.problem:
Find the equation of the osculating plane (in parametric form) for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+{t}^{3}\,k,\,T(0)=i,\,N(0)=j.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-78207.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point that is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$ The vectors $T(0)$ and $N(0)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, the equation of the plane (in parametric form) can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =0\,i+{0}^{2}\,j+{0}^{3}\,k=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the osculating plane at the point $(0,0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0) \\  & =0+s(i)+u(j) \\  & =s\,i+u\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

q-78207.html:
Question 4
?

Find the equation of the osculating plane (in parametric form) for the curve r(t) at the point where t=0, given that

r(t)=ti+t2j+t3k,T(0)=i,N(0)=j.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
 R(s,u)=si+sj+uk
b
 R(s,u)=si+(s+u)j+uk
c
 R(s,u)=(1+s)i+(1+u)j+uk
d
 R(s,u)=(1+s)i+(1+u)k
e
R(s,u)=si+uj
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The osculating plane passes through the point that is at the tip of the vector r(0). The vectors T(0) and N(0) are parallel to this plane. Therefore, the equation of the plane (in parametric form) can be written as

R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0),s,u∈(−∞,∞).

We have that r(0)=0i+02j+03k=0.

Hence, the equation of the osculating plane at the point (0,0,0) is given by

R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0)=0+s(i)+u(j)=si+uj.

q-34082.name: Question 5
q-34082.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\pi $, given that

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,T(\pi )=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨1,0,-1⟩,\,N(\pi )=⟨0,1,0⟩.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-34082.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P$, which is at the tip of the vector $r(\pi ).$ The vectors $T(\pi )$ and $N(\pi )$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(\pi )+s\,T(\pi )+u\,N(\pi ),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨\pi ,-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(\pi ,-1,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(\pi )+s\,T(\pi )+u\,N(\pi ) \\  & =⟨\pi ,-1,0⟩+s\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨1,0,-1⟩+u\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨2\pi +\sqrt{2}s,\,-2+2u,\,-\sqrt{2}s⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-34082.html:
Question 5
?

Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve r(t) at the point where t=π, given that

r(t)=⟨t,cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩,T(π)=22⟨1,0,−1⟩,N(π)=⟨0,1,0⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
R(s,u)=⟨−2+2u,−2s,2⟩
b
R(s,u)=12⟨2π+2s,−2+2u,−2s⟩
c
R(s,u)=⟨−2,2π+2s,−2s⟩
d
R(s,u)=12⟨−2s,2π,−2+2u⟩
e
R(s,u)=12⟨0,−2s,−π+u⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The osculating plane passes through the point P, which is at the tip of the vector r(π). The vectors T(π) and N(π) are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

R(s,u)=r(π)+sT(π)+uN(π),s,u∈(−∞,∞).

We have that

r(π)=⟨π,cos⁡π,sin⁡π⟩=⟨π,−1,0⟩.

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point (π,−1,0) is given by

R(s,u)=r(π)+sT(π)+uN(π)=⟨π,−1,0⟩+s⋅22⟨1,0,−1⟩+u⋅⟨0,1,0⟩=12⟨2π+2s,−2+2u,−2s⟩.

q-33665.name: Question 6
q-33665.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{t}^{2}\,k \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{3}\,k) \\ N(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-33665.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=0$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{3}\,k)=\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k \\ N(0) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,j=j.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
p=r(0)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡0+(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0)\,i+(\operatorname{sin}⁡0-(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0)\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(0)^{2}\,k=⟨1,0,0⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =(\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k)\times j \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=2\cdot (T(0)\times N(0))=-\sqrt{3}\,i+k=⟨-\sqrt{3},0,1⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-\sqrt{3},0,1⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨-\sqrt{3},0,1⟩ \\ -\sqrt{3}\cdot x+0\cdot y+1\cdot z & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3}x-z-\sqrt{3} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-33691.name: Question 7
q-33691.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1,1)$ where $t=0$, given that

$$
T(0)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(\,i+\,j+\,k),\,N(0)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\,i-\,j).
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-33691.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(0,1,1)$ is $p=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

To find the equation of the osculating plane, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to it. To do that, we find the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(\,i+\,j+\,k))\times (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\,i-\,j)) \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}(i+j-2\,k)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=\sqrt{6}\cdot (T(0)\times N(0))=i+j-2\,k=⟨1,1,-2⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a general point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,-2⟩ & =⟨0,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,-2⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+1\cdot y+(-2)\cdot z & =-1 \\ x+y-2z & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, our perpendicular vector $n$ is 

$$
n=T(0)\times N(0)=⟨0,-1,0⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,-1,0⟩ & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\cdot ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\ x(0)+y(-1)+z(0) & =0(0)+2(-1)+(-1)(0) \\ 0-y+0 & =0-2+0 \\ y-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-33782.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(1,0,0)$ where $t=1$, given that

$$
T(1)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\,i+\,j),\,N(1)=k.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-33782.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(1,0,0)$ is $p=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

To find the equation of the osculating plane, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to it. To do that, we find the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\times N(1) & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\,i+\,j))\times k \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=\sqrt{2}\cdot (T(1)\times N(1))=i-j=⟨1,-1,0⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a general point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+0\cdot z & =1 \\ x-y-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

q-79231.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(4,0,4)$ where $t=-2$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(-2) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-1,\,\sqrt{2},\,1⟩ \\ N(-2) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-79231.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(4,0,4)$ is $p=⟨4,\,0,\,4⟩.$

We need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(-2)$ and the principal normal $N(-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(-2)\times N(-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-1,\,\sqrt{2},\,1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & \sqrt{2} & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}(\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j-\sqrt{2}\,k) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨1,\sqrt{2},-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨4,0,4⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨1,\sqrt{2},-1⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}|4+0-4| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79234.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{2}+\sqrt{2})\,i+(\sqrt{2}-{t}^{2})\,j+2t\,k \\ T(0) & =k \\ N(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-79234.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
p=r(0)=(0+\sqrt{2})\,i+(\sqrt{2}-0)\,j+0\,k=⟨\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2},0⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(0)\times N(0) \\  & =k\times (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-\,j)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2},0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,1,0⟩| \\  & =|1+1| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-127314.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(1,-1,5)$ where $t=0,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨-2,-1,3⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
q-127314.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(1,-1,5)$ is $p=i-j+5\,k.$

We need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(0)\times N(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨-2,-1,3⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{42}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{42}}[\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{42}}(-4\,i+5\,j-\,k)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|(i-j+5\,k)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{42}}(-4\,i+5\,j-\,k)| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{42}}|-4-5-5| \\  & =\frac{|-14|}{\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{42}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨0,-1,1⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,3⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}|\,0-4+3\,| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}

Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve r(t) at the point where t=−π, given that

r(t)=⟨sin3⁡t,cos3⁡t,cos⁡2t⟩T(−π)=15⟨0,3,−4⟩N(−π)=⟨−1,0,0⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
 1
b
 15
c
 5
d
 110
e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the position vector of the point where t=−π is p=r(−π)=⟨sin3⁡(−π),cos3⁡(−π),cos⁡(−2π)⟩=⟨0,−1,1⟩.

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent T(−π) and the principal normal N(−π):

T(−π)×N(−π)=15⟨0,3,−4⟩×⟨−1,0,0⟩=15ijk03−4−100=15[ 3−400i−0−4−10j+03−10k ]=15⟨0,4,3⟩

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by d=|(p−0)⋅n|‖n‖=|p⋅n|‖n‖=|p⋅n|, since ‖n‖=1. Therefore, we have

d=|p⋅n|=|⟨0,−1,1⟩⋅15⟨0,4,3⟩|=15|0−4+3|=15.
